runs.reason:

That is the starting point for an initiative before considering its polling. ([bk.admin.ch](https://www.bk.admin.ch/dam/en/sd-web/KYXe43NjDhNT/The%20Swiss%20Confederation.%20A%20brief%20guide%202026.pdf?trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block))

**What moves this case.** Three November polls move it sharply toward YES: gfs.bern measured 63% support, LeeWas 62%, and YouGov 59%. The support was not confined to cities: gfs.bern found 59% support in rural communities and a Yes majority in all three language regions, while YouGov’s canton-level model showed Yes ahead almost everywhere. That geographic breadth matters more for the double majority than another point or two in the national polls. ([srf.ch](https://www.srf.ch/news/zweite-srg-umfrage-feuerwerksinitiative-ja-anteil-schrumpft-erfolgschancen-nicht?utm_source=openai))

**What could go wrong.** Support fell six points between gfs.bern’s two waves, and the November 27 reporting still described an active No campaign backed by the Federal Council and Parliament. A further swing concentrated in smaller cantons could cost the initiative the cantonal majority even if it wins nationally. I put the chance of the vote not taking place on November 29 below 1%: the Federal Statistical Office has scheduled live reporting from noon, and the November 27 coverage still confirms the date. ([srf.ch](https://www.srf.ch/news/zweite-srg-umfrage-feuerwerksinitiative-ja-anteil-schrumpft-erfolgschancen-nicht?utm_source=openai))

Because Swiss voters predominantly cast their ballots by mail over the two to three weeks preceding voting Sunday, a substantial fraction of ballots were already cast while the initiative polled around 60–63%. Nevertheless, with ~45–49% support even among SVP and FDP voters and ~60% overall support in mid-November, losing 12 cantons would require an unprecedented late rural swing of roughly 10–12 percentage points.

runs.reason:
The unconditional historical acceptance rate for Swiss popular initiatives is low, near one in ten, because most fail to clear both the popular majority and the cantonal majority (more than 11.5 of 23). That base rate is a poor guide once late, large-sample polls show a settled double-digit lead with only mild regional variation: such initiatives usually clear both hurdles.

The vote is fixed for 29 November 2026. The second SRG/gfs.bern survey (fieldwork 4–11 November, published 18 November) put intending voters at 63% yes and 35% no, with 78% already firm and 52% definite yes—already a popular majority on its own. The same wave still showed majorities in every language region (German-speaking Switzerland 65%, French-speaking 57%, Italian-speaking 53%) and in rural municipalities (59%). A contemporaneous Tamedia reading was 62% yes. Support had fallen six points since mid-October, and it had slipped among FDP and SVP sympathisers toward their parties’ no line, but the remaining cushion is large and the geographic split is not sharp.

The popular majority therefore looks very secure. The residual risk is almost entirely the cantonal majority if the late slide continues and is concentrated in small conservative cantons and in Latin Switzerland.
